extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent litigators, patent attorneys, and IP practitioners involved in claim construction and patent case management (international comparative audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative guidance and standards for how courts handle claim construction and related procedural management in patent litigation (timing, evidence, rulings, bifurcation, functional claims, and sanctions). Draws on practices from multiple national courts (US, Germany, Japan, Korea, China).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markman Hearing (judge-led claim construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Markman Hearing: judges have responsibility for determining disputes over terms and claims (originating from Markman v. Westview). Timing is discretionary (no set rule from CAFC or Supreme Court); it is left to the district judge's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical practice (Judge Sleet): schedule at or near close of fact discovery, before expert reports are due and before close of expert discovery; oral argument is interactive (not like appellate argument); judges may attempt to steer parties toward agreement during the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic Evidence Hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification/written description, prosecution history) is to be given the highest value in claim construction (per Philips); extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, technical manuals, expert declarations/testimony) is secondary and not exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many judges confine discussion to the intrinsic record; extrinsic evidence can be useful (e.g., dictionaries), but judges often avoid expert testimony/declarations as litigation-driven. There are no absolute rules—courts weigh usefulness and may exclude extrinsic evidence depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of Separate Procedure for Claim Construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether courts provide a separate procedure for claim construction in infringement suits varies by jurisdiction: some (e.g., some US practices) have separate Markman proceedings; many jurisdictions handle claim construction together with validity and infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision often depends on case complexity: complex patents may require separate claim-construction hearings during pre-trial; simple physical-object cases may be resolved together with infringement/validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate Claim Construction Ruling vs Preliminary View vs Integrated Ruling
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may issue a separate claim construction order (brief order), a full opinion, or a preliminary view disclosed at oral hearing; some jurisdictions issue no separate ruling but may disclose preliminary views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders (Judge Sleet) are brief, issued quickly (e.g., ~30 days), and explain reasoning succinctly to aid parties and appellate courts; German courts give a preliminary view at the start of oral hearing to indicate tendencies and allow a last chance to respond; preliminary views can be changed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage procedure (first stage: claim construction/infringement; second stage: damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems (e.g., Japan) operate a two-stage process where the court first resolves infringement/claim-construction issues and only if infringement is found proceeds to damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This front-loaded approach permits early termination if no infringement is found and promotes efficiency; when infringement is likely, courts disclose opinion and ask parties to submit damages evidence for the second stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of Claim Construction to Bifurcated Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is generally the first step regardless of whether a jurisdiction uses a bifurcated system (separate courts for validity and infringement) or unitary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in bifurcated systems, claim construction must be understood first to focus later infringement or validity analysis; where courts differ, later courts should give reasons if they depart from prior determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of Claim Construction Criteria between Validity and Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the same interpretive criteria apply in validity and infringement decisions varies: some jurisdictions/practices apply the same criteria; others historically applied more restrictive constructions in infringement to avoid overbroad protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Korea nominally applies same criteria but Supreme Court guidance allows restrictive constructions in infringement when literal construction is 'clearly unreasonable'; Japan's Kilby decision and later case law trend toward using the same interpretation for both validity and infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Claims: contrasting standards (patent office vs. courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent offices (e.g., SIPO) and patent reexamination bodies may interpret function-defined features broadly ('embracing all the means capable of performing the function'), while courts typically construe functional features narrowly based on specific embodiments in the description/drawings or equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SIPO/Patent Office guidelines prefer avoiding functional features in product claims unless necessary; function-based claim language is permissible only if supported by description, experimentally verifiable, and not so broad as to include means that cannot solve the technical problem. Courts may limit functional claims to the embodiments disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility / Support Requirement for Functional Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim element defined purely by function is permissible only if the function is supported by the description and the person skilled in the art can understand how to implement it; unsupported pure-functional definitions are not allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If embodiments show a particular way of implementing the function, a skilled person may not assume other alternatives exist; examiners/courts will reject function claims that increase speculative alternatives or include means incapable of solving the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction: question of law vs. mixed question (fact/law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is often treated as a question of law, but subsidiary fact-finding (e.g., about facts necessary to construe terms, or the perspective/knowledge of the person skilled in the art) may occur and be reviewed for clear error (per Teva).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different jurisdictions/levels treat this differently: CAFC historically treated it as law with de novo review; Teva requires clear-error review for factual findings made by district courts. Judges may therefore engage in some fact-finding but expect appellate review standards to differ for pure law vs. factual subsidiary findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's use of 'person skilled in the art' and need for factual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting what a claim means may require assessing the perspective/abilities of a person skilled in the art (a legal 'dummy'); this may necessitate factual inquiry to determine education, skills, and knowledge of that hypothetical person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual aspects can 'sneak in' through this lens; courts may take evidence (dictionaries, expert descriptions) to determine the skilled person's approach, but still frame the ultimate decision as legal construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Case Management Special Rules (front-loading and timetables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions/districts have special patent case management rules or guidelines (e.g., Northern District of California, District of New Jersey, certain Chinese provisions); others (e.g., Delaware district courts) rely on robust Rule 16 case-management orders rather than formal patent-specific rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where present, guidelines set expectations for submission timing (e.g., claimant's arguments/evidence by first preparation date, defendant's counters by second date) and seek rapid resolution (e.g., IP High Court aiming to conclude appeals in 7–8 months). In jurisdictions without formal rules, judges use scheduling conferences, pre-trial proceedings, and designation-of-pleading-date orders to front-load and manage patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order for preparation / mandatory pre-submission of terms and technology slides
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may issue preparation orders requiring parties to submit terms/phrases to be construed, technology explanations (slides), and desired claim terms before the first trial/hearing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These orders facilitate focused early claim construction and limit surprise; failure to comply with such orders may lead to exclusion of late materials absent good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary view disclosure (Germany) and opportunity to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: German courts may give a preliminary view after deliberation and before oral hearing (not limited to claim construction) to indicate tentative interpretation/finding and allow parties a 'last chance' to address the points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary views are not final and can be changed; the purpose is to signal the court's provisional thinking and permit corrective input from the parties rather than to provoke them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for Failing to Meet Time Limits and Exceptions (admission of late allegations/evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations or evidence submitted late are generally not admitted; exceptions exist where late submission was not intentional or not due to gross negligence, or where admissibility is necessary to avoid a party losing the whole case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges assess whether 'all due care' was taken (e.g., hospitalization after accident can justify extension). Practical handling varies: courts may dismiss or ignore late submissions, or in some cases admit them if they concern 'basic facts' (e.g., prior art) or if strict exclusion would be unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence Related to Basic Facts Exception (China)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese practice: even where law says evidence provided beyond time limit should be inadmissible, evidence 'related to basic facts' shall be regarded admissible; such evidence is that without which the submitting party would lose the whole case (e.g., prior art or design evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception recognizes that certain late evidence goes to the core of entitlement; courts exercise discretion to admit such evidence despite procedural default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration of Asserted Claims During First-instance Debate (China)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Chinese interpretations, where a right holder alters the claim asserted by him before the end of the court debate of the first instance, the court shall permit such alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule allows parties to adjust assertions during early stages to reflect issues developed in litigation; timing (before end of debate) is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial disclosure of infringement opinion to promote settlement (Japan practice described)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some jurisdictions (example given for Japan), if the court thinks there is infringement it will disclose that opinion at the end of the first stage and then ask parties to proceed to damages argument; this disclosure can encourage settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merits: time/cost efficiency and increased chance of settlement because defendants better assess risk upon knowing court's inclination on infringement; such disclosure may operate like a near-final decision for purposes of case strategy.
